slides: Okay, planning the essay. Step one: analysing the task.
Before we look for even one argument, we need to understand exactly what they're asking us... and what kind of task it is.
So, when we sit down to write an essay, the first thing we do is... not write.
The first thing we do is analyse the task.
Here's the example task we already know. Face-recognition cameras in public spaces.
If you need to, stop the video for a moment and read it again.
So how do we analyse it? Well, with a few fixed questions. Let's go through them one by one.
The first question: is the interest the same, or is it different?
It's like we walk up to the two sides and ask them, why are you arguing? What do you actually want?
Maybe they both want the same thing, and each one just wants to get there in a different way. A common goal. A similar interest.
Or maybe each side has a different interest, and each one is looking after itself.
Now, our cameras. Why are you arguing? Well, the state wants to look after security. And people want to protect their privacy.
So here, the interests are different.
Now another task. Should a minister be an expert in the ministry's field, or an elected public representative?
One side says, an expert. The other says, no way, an elected representative. And I say, wait, wait. What do you both want?
You both want the minister to be effective. To do the job as well as possible. So you're not enemies. You're actually friends, with a common goal.
Each of you just thinks there's a different way to get there.
And this helps us later, both when we look for arguments, and when we weaken the other side's arguments.
The second thing. We want to see the big picture, to understand what's really going on here. A kind of zoom out.
The situation they describe is one particular case of something bigger. And it's that bigger thing we're meant to discuss.
I mean, you could build the same debate from lots of different situations. This is just the one they use to lead us into it.
So what's the big picture with the cameras? It's a debate about security against privacy.
You could take many other situations that bring security and privacy together. This is just one particular case of that clash.
Now, another point worth noticing.
When the state is one of the sides in the dispute, very often it's a clash of rights.
Not always, okay? Not every dispute is a clash of rights. There are all kinds of disputes.
But if the state is involved, it'll usually be about rights. Why? Well, what is the state, actually?
It's not just a private person doing whatever it likes. It's there to protect the citizens, the people who live there. To protect our rights.
So if the state is involved, it's probably looking after some right of the citizens.
And in our task? The state is involved, and it fits perfectly. It's a clash between the right to security and the right to privacy.
The next thing I check is probably the most important part of analysing a task. We call it the choice axis.
Obviously, in any situation, in any dispute, each side has advantages and disadvantages.
And in exam tasks, things are more or less balanced. There won't be one side with almost only advantages. That task just wouldn't appear, because there's nothing to argue about.
So what do we do? We draw an axis. Our choice axis, between against and for.
And we place ourselves on it. I say, well, I think there are more advantages on the side of for. So I put myself somewhere here.
I'm not completely for, because I understand this position has disadvantages too. So I'm not all the way at the end. But I'm closer to for.
Now let's look at the kinds of tasks. Because where you can stand on the axis depends on the kind of task.
Some tasks are yes or no. And there, we choose the side we're closer to.
For example, should the office of president be abolished, or not?
Even if I understand there are advantages and disadvantages to keeping it or abolishing it, even if it's not black and white... in the end, I have to decide.
I mean, there can't be half a president. Or a quarter of a president.
So I choose the side I'm closer to. I think keeping it has more advantages, so I choose for the office of president. I choose the end.
Some tasks we call degree tasks. And there, it's not exactly about the ends.
For example: to what extent should we rely on public transport?
They're not asking me whether to rely on public transport, yes or no. They're asking, to what extent?
So if I think only a little, I say, rely on it a little. Or I say, yes, a lot. We should rely on it heavily.
I can put myself anywhere along the whole axis.
We call this an obvious degree task, because, well, it's clear. They're asking me, to what extent.
But sometimes we get hidden degree tasks. And these are actually very common.
For example: should a bonus be included in an employee's pay? It sounds like a yes or no question, right?
But it isn't, exactly. Here too, there's a degree hidden inside.
We have an absolute end, and a flexible end. No is the absolute end. No bonus, we don't give the employee a bonus, that's it. There's nowhere to move.
But if I do want to give a bonus, then I have a flexible end. Wait, how much bonus? Just a little? A big part of the pay? A small part? Only on sales above a certain amount?
I can move along the whole axis. A small bonus, only on small things... or mostly bonus, because that motivates people the most.
So it's also a degree task. It's just worded as yes or no. And it's very important to notice these hidden degree tasks.
We'll come back to this when we talk about the considerations for choosing a position.
Now, there are also tasks that aren't for and against in the classic way.
For example: why is it worth learning to play an instrument at a young age?
It sounds like, hmm, what's this? A different task? It's not an argument essay, it's not for and against.
But really, it is. It's an ordinary for-and-against task. They just chose the position for you in advance.
I could have asked the same task like this: should children learn an instrument at a young age? Yes or no. But I turned it into, why is it worth it.
And by the way, I can turn almost any task into a why task. Why is it worth installing face-recognition cameras in public spaces?
So what did I do? I chose your side for you, and now I want you to explain it.
Bottom line, no need to get stressed about a why task. They saved you the hesitation. Just carry on from there.
In most cases, we're used to two opinions. One for, and one against. But sometimes there are three.
Then we need to check. Is it two ends and a middle, or is it three different options?
For example: should an employee's pay be only a base salary, only a bonus, meaning only a percentage of sales, or both?
That's two ends and a middle. One end, only base. The other end, only bonus. And the middle, both.
Now, toll roads. Who should pay, and how? Well, you can pay per trip. That sounds fair. Whoever uses it more, pays more.
Or you can pay for a monthly or yearly pass. Then people who use it a lot pay less per trip, and people who use it a little end up paying more per trip.
Or the state can pay for it. Then all the citizens pay for the trips of the people who use the road.
Here there's no middle. Each opinion is completely different.
These are rarer. And we'll see in the recommended structures that it's still just an ordinary argument essay.
Now, one more step, and it's a big one. Answer exactly the question they asked.
Before you start looking for reasons, find three things in the question.
One, the decision. What exactly is being decided? Two, the people. Who exactly is affected? And three, the conditions that must stay true.
So in our task, the decision is whether to allow the security services to install face-recognition cameras in public spaces. Not in private homes. Not cameras in general.
An essay can sound very thoughtful and still talk about the wrong issue. And that's not a small wording problem. It's a problem in your thinking.
If you quietly change the decision, the people, or the setting... you've answered a different question. And that's exactly what weak essays do.
Let's practise on a new task.
Read it. So what's the decision? Switching off the lights in residential streets, between one and five at night. Not all night. And not on main roads.
Who's affected? The people who live in those streets. Especially people who come home late, like night-shift workers, and elderly residents. The task names them.
Now, if I write a paragraph about how dark main roads cause car accidents, well, I've changed the setting. The main roads stay lit. So I'm answering a different question.
So before every paragraph, check. Same decision? Same people? Same conditions?
And one more rule. Every part of the question needs an answer.
Look at this question. Advantages and disadvantages. For the residents, and for the city itself.
So that's really four boxes. Advantages for residents, disadvantages for residents, advantages for the city, and disadvantages for the city.
A brilliant essay about the residents alone leaves half the task unfinished.
So the plan of your essay comes from what the question asks. Not from some shape you memorised.
The official guide says it too. A good essay directly addresses all elements of the task.
